speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, I seek to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head V of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is good news for Singapore as it meant more economic activities, better jobs opportunities, more tax revenues to strengthen our fiscal position and better standard of living for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Credit to Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) and our economic agencies for managing our economy well to achieve the above-trend growth despite our inherent domestic constraints.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The question is: can we do it again in 2025?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How important is it for us to push for higher growth; beyond the 1% to 3% range?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Economic growth creates good jobs and helps sustain real wage growth for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A more vibrant economy invigorates the business ecosystem and generate business opportunities for the enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In our context, having a strong and growing economy enable us to stay plugged to the global trade and investments flows; and also enable Singapore to stay closely abreast of new developments and advancements in the growth frontiers areas, such as the advance manufacturing, innovations and digital space and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a growing economy also allows us to participate in the global supply chains and enhances our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, having a sizeable and growing economy helps us stay relevant internationally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines are not far behind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It imperative that we continue to seek growth; be it a more moderate pace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Back to my earlier point whether we can and should grow beyond the 1% to 3%. range, I would say let us always strive to pick up that additional 0.5% to 1% of growth where we can.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To do that, it requires us to steadfastly work on overcoming our tight constraints on land and workforce and now also carbon.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To create new capacities for higher growth, the hard truth is that we need structural productivity improvements to create new growth capacities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This includes pressing on with enterprise transformations, skills upgrade and continual infrastructural build-up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this Budget and earlier Budgets, a number of support schemes have been introduced and many enhanced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to differentiate with our other value propositions, such as the availability of educated and skilled workforce, our world class infrastructure, our premier status as a financial centre, our reputable legal system and our pro-business environment, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One area of strategic importance and where we can differentiate is to bolster Singapore's position as centre of excellences for technological and innovation developments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It enables us to attract cutting-edge high performing companies to Singapore and to anchor value here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Semiconductors and biomedical sciences are among the high-performing sectors that we should target and to build an ecosystem conducive for its developments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our next bound of economic growth can also come from strengthening our position as a global hub for startups and innovation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Gearing up our enterprises to embrace AI solutions are also necessary enablers to achieve productivity improvements and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Productivity Solutions Grant and SMEs Go Digital schemes already assist enterprises to utilise off-the-shelf solutions for marketing and business analytics.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this year's Budget, the support is extended to more customise solutions tailored to the enterprises' needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a meaningful new initiative and can help companies develop new use cases and commercially viable and creative applications as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I look forward to more details of this scheme later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I suggest that besides partnering the cloud service providers, I hope that MTI can also include our local institutions of higher learning (IHLs) and their students to help enterprises develop tailored solutions and commercial use cases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These could be structured as IHLs' industry projects and/or as internship opportunities for the students, so that our IHLs and students are also able to participate in industries' AI developments and to keep their curriculums relevant and updated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What could be the worst-case scenario for us?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Against this backdrop, of trade and technology decoupling, how would the re-organising of the supply chain impact the future of Singapore's manufacturing sector?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How would MTI ensure that manufacturing continues to be a key pillar of our economy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In that heated exchange, the Ukrainian President was told, "he has no cards to play".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is a sobering reminder that, as a country, we must never be caught in a situation where we have no cards to play.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, our economy has long thrived on our ability to remain open, connected and deeply integrated into the global trade networks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In recent years and, in fact, weeks and days, protectionist measures and escalating geopolitical conflicts across major nations have become the norm.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are at a precarious crossroads as a small, open economy where commerce accounts for over three times our GDP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have also seen first-hand how conflicts, such as the Russian-Ukraine war, have caused inflationary pressures on the cost of living globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share the impact of global geopolitical tensions on Singapore's trade relations with other countries and our strategy for navigating this?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What strategies will the Ministry utilise to ensure that we can adeptly navigate an increasingly fragmented global economy?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Concurrently, we remain committed to our resolve to strengthen global trade relations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, participation in platforms, such as the ASEAN's Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership is vital in our mission to encourage closer regional cooperation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share our efforts in working with our global neighbours or, in fact, regional ones, to avoid the fragmentation of the global economy?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sustained economic success is dependent on our ability to remain nimble, adjusting our trade strategies in tandem with the ever-changing geopolitical landscape.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is hence imperative for us to ensure our trade strategies are resilient and responsive to opportunities and uncertainties to ensure our economic success beyond SG60.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Countries have responded with retaliatory tariffs as well as tried to delay and negotiate the way after the rollout.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But just yesterday, stocks tumbled, as President Trump announced that he is moving forward with the proposed tariffs, adding that time had run out to reach a deal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More tariffs are expected to be announced in the coming months.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But what is clear is that all companies will be affected.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These, alongside other geopolitical uncertainties like increased protectionism, non-tariff barriers, such as subsidies and export controls, and disruptions caused by climate change, technological changes, among others, as well as changes in security of the world, will make companies reassess their supplier base and their own footprint.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What assessment has MTI made of the potential impact scenarios on key sectors like manufacturing and Singapore's overall position as a global hub, and what responses are being planned?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The convergence of geopolitical tensions, the US-China trade war, strategic competition in artificial intelligence (AI), and political realignments are reshaping the global economy, supply chains and technological deployment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore, as a small, open economy, is particularly sensitive to these shifts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The tariffs have disrupted global supply chains, leading to uncertainty and volatility in markets.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The rivalry is so strong that the US and China are willing to risk hurting their own economies, and one can imagine small countries like us can become unfortunate collateral damage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Then, there is also the strategic competition in AI, exemplified by China's advancements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This rivalry contributes to geopolitical tensions, influencing global trade policies and economic alliances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I had spoken on this during my Budget Debate speech and will do so again at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information's (MDDI's) Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore's economy relies heavily on global trade and investment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This sector relies on the seamless flow of raw materials, components and finished goods across borders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our deep integration with the global supply chain ensured our economic success but can also make us vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, changes in external demand, supply chain reorganisation and shifting geoeconomic landscape will certainly have an outsized impact on our economy and, ultimately, livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As such, considering these macro factors and impact, what are MTI's plans to build resilience into our supply chains and manufacturing sector?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How might our manufacturing sector shape up looking ahead?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One way to build resilience is to ensure that trading partners' interests and ours continue to remain aligned.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Put bluntly, to deepen their invested interests in us and ours in them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now that the multilateral trading system is under pressure, how is MTI working to strengthen our trade links with the region and the world?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can MTI provide more details on how we intend to diversify our trading partners amidst the trade tensions, and how Singapore companies can benefit from these partnerships?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, geopolitical tensions, trade policy shifts and technological advancements are driving significant changes in the global trade landscape.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The concept of reglobalisation is emerging as businesses seek to create more resilient and adaptable supply chains.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The US-China trade dispute has significantly impacted global trade as trade between the two countries has decreased.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Companies are also diversifying their production capacities to other markets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from tariffs, weather conditions, geopolitical conflicts and cybersecurity concerns have made supply chains increasingly complex.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Against this geoeconomic landscape, businesses need to adapt.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They need to rethink their sourcing, production and delivery strategies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are diversifying their supplier base, investing in more stable regions if there is something more stable these days, and adopting innovative strategies to build more resilient and responsive supply chains.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What impact will this have on the future of Singapore's manufacturing sector, and what are MTI's plans to ensure that manufacturing continues to be a key pillar of our economy?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, global supply chains are being reorganised amid shifting geoeconomic dynamics, presenting both challenges and opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As competition for high-value manufacturing investments intensifies, it is critical that we safeguard our position as a leading advanced manufacturing hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What impact will these global shifts have on the future of Singapore's manufacturing sector and how is MTI ensuring that manufacturing remains a key pillar of our economy?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, what measures are in place to strengthen our supply chain resilience, attract high-value investments, and deepen our local talent pipeline to secure good jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given the increased focus on automation, sustainability and regional diversification, how will Singapore position itself to stay ahead in the evolving global manufacturing landscape?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, since a long time pre-Independence, our geographical centrality has made trade the lifeblood of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the world's multilateral trading system is coming under real pressure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During President Trump's first presidential term, the United States (US) withdrew from the Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the risks of the imposition of specific and reciprocal tariffs by the US on our major trading partners likely to affect Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the current backdrop, how is MTI working to strengthen our trade links with the region and the world?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can MTI elaborate on how we intend to diversify our trading partners amidst the trade tensions, and how Singapore companies can benefit from these partnerships?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the technology and innovation engines mentioned in Budget 2025 hews closely to our manufacturing Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs), namely, for precision engineering, energy and chemicals, marine and offshore, aerospace and electronics.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Added to this is the uncertainty of how global supply chains are being restructured, as a result of vulnerabilities that had been exposed by COVID-19, geopolitical tensions in specific regions and changes in the national priorities of particular countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What impact will the Johor-Singapore SEZ and changes to the global supply chains have on the future of Singapore's manufacturing sector and other sectors, and what are MTI's plans to ensure that manufacturing continues to be a key pillar of our economy and also how can we take advantage of opportunities as companies and global companies reallocate their supply chains from other places?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is especially so as Singapore, with her limited land and resources, can ill afford an unchecked rise in e-waste, or, in fact, any waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The disposal of electronics in landfills result in hazardous pollutants, while the constant need for new products strains our supply chains and increases reliance on raw material extraction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Addressing planned obsolescence and promoting the right to repair are crucial steps towards a secular economy and long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It does not go far enough in tackling planned obsolescence or ensuring consumers can repair their devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are no laws penalising manufacturers for intentionally shortening product lifespans, nor do we have regulations guaranteeing access to spare parts or repair manuals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many Singaporeans have experienced the frustration of purchasing an affordable product online, only to have it malfunction within a short time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Without access to spare parts or repair options, consumers are left with no recourse but to dispose of the faulty item and buy a replacement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This not only wastes money but also contributes to unnecessary waste.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A right to repair framework would address such common consumer grievances by ensuring that products are repairable and that manufacturers provide the necessary support for maintenance and longevity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This index requires manufacturers to assign a repairability score to their products, ranging from one to 10.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: France also banned intentionally shortening the lifespan of products and imposes heavy fines on companies engaging in planned obsolescence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A phone or vacuum cleaner that lasts four years instead of two would half the electronic waste across time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Sweden introduced tax incentive to make the repair of goods more affordable for consumers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Valued-Added Tax (VAT) on repair services for items, such as bicycles, shoes and clothing was halved from 25% to 12%, effectively lowering the cost of these services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Additionally, consumers can claim back from income tax half the labour cost of compliance repairs performed by technicians in their home, up to a certain limit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These measures are designed to make repairing goods more financially attractive than replacing them, thereby extending product lifespan and reducing environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By making repairs more economically viable, there is an increased demand for skilled technicians and repair services, leading to job creation and the growth of small businesses specialising in maintenance and refurbishment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By adopting similar right to repair laws, Singapore can enhance consumer rights, reduce electronic waste and foster a more resilient economy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Additionally, an independent consumer advocacy body should be set up to monitor and report cases of planned obsolescence, ensuring transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Transparency and access to information are key to empowering consumers to make informed choices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A mandatory repairability rating system prominently displayed on product packaging would enable consumers to compare products based on their expected longevity and ease of repair.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would help consumers avoid purchasing products with artificially short life spans, ultimately leading to more sustainable consumption habits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Additionally, public education campaigns can be launched to raise awareness about repair rights and available services, ensuring that consumers are equipped with the knowledge to extend the life of their products.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Responsible businesses that already prioritise product quality, longevity and repairability would benefit from increased consumer trust and brand loyalty over businesses that rely on planned obsolescence to drive sales.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By fostering a market where durability and sustainability are rewarded, we can shift industry standards towards more ethical and environmental friendly practices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, my cut today is focused on consumer protection for online scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to why I am filing this card for MTI instead of other more obviously connected Ministries, this is because I believe that the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore can play a major role in this area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, I wish to acknowledge the work of the different agencies, some around the clock, to prevent, detect, disrupt and respond to online scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, the Shared Responsibility Framework falls under the purview of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, as an integrated financial regulator with a focus on prudential oversight and supervision of the financial services sector, it would be difficult to expect the MAS to also protect and enforce consumer rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Consumer complaints are often directed to channels, such as the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDRec) or the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE), but both have limitations, including in enforcement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, the current approach also means that solutions like the Shared Responsibility Framework, which is currently limited to phishing scams, only apply to banks and telcos.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Consumers need a stronger advocate in their fight against scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CCCS is a statutory board and has the power and legal authority to set and enforce national consumer protection standards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Critically, it will be able to protect consumer rights across a range of sectors and be a single point of contact for scam victims seeking redress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has recently been done in Australia with the passage of the Scams Prevention Framework Bill 2025.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill established the framework within the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, and under the supervision of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As noted by the Minister at the Second Reading of that Bill, the legislation operates across a whole range of sectors, including social media platforms, and allows consumers to look at a trusted, centralised point within Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our approach would be strengthened by having a centralised consumer protection agency, like CCCS, set and enforce such standards across a range of sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: E-commerce has fundamentally changed the way consumers shop, creating new consumer protection concerns and exacerbating existing unfair business practices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Budget debate speech, I spoke at length about the importance of ensuring that our consumer protection regime and legislation are updated and remain fit-for-purpose in this e-commerce era.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is the Ministry’s plan to tighten and enhance consumer protection for Singaporean consumers, who are increasingly turning to e-commerce?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In parallel, the Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) for Pro-Enterprise Rules Review was formed to ensure that regulations remain agile, business-friendly and aligned with Singapore’s economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Can MTI provide an update on the progress of the IMC and the SME PEO, and how these initiatives are working together to streamline processes, reduce compliance costs and ensure that pro-enterprise policies translate into real benefits for SMEs?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How will these efforts help Singapore businesses stay competitive amidst rising costs and global headwinds?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in February 2024, MTI and the Singapore Business Federation launched a bold collaboration – the Alliance for Action on Business Competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These recommendations serve not merely as proposals but as a roadmap to transform obstacles into opportunities, whether through diversifying our talent pool, extending industrial land lease tenures or streamlining regulatory processes.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This committee is focused on reducing compliance costs and easing regulatory burdens, particularly for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This one-stop centre promises to be a game-changer by providing direct, hands-on support to businesses navigating complex regulations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, these initiatives underscore our strong commitment to cultivating a vibrant and competitive business environment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Second, how will the SME Pro-Enterprise Office engage with businesses to alleviate regulatory challenges and integrate their feedback to keep our framework agile and responsive?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, to operate a business in Singapore involves compliance with several ongoing regulatory requirements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Depending on the business sector, there may be additional sector-specific mandatory compliance requirements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With businesses, especially smaller businesses, facing increasing business costs, what efforts are being made by the Government to simplify and streamline rules and regulations to reduce compliance costs for businesses?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, businesses need to continue to manage costs efficiently, especially in a competitive environment.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned by Members previously, can MTI provide an update on the the IMC for Pro-Enterprise Rules Review and the SME Pro-Enterprise Office (PEO).

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore’s next phase of economic growth hinges on reinforcing our position as a global hub for startups and innovation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Despite a strong entrepreneurship ecosystem, startups continue to face challenges in securing growth funding, with valuations under pressure and increased dilutions for founders and employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond capital, networks are crucial in scaling enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Strong global networks enable startups and high-growth enterprises to internationalise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How is MTI fostering an ecosystem where personal networks support enterprise scaling?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As Singapore strengthens its status as a global wealth hub, many high-net-worth individuals possess vast business networks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How is MTI engaging these individuals to deploy patient capital and activate their networks to help local enterprises expand internationally?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our commitment to net-zero by 2050 requires decisive action, particularly in decarbonising the power sector.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Higher renewable energy costs may impact business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MTI provide an update on strategies to ensure a sustainable transition while maintaining economic competitiveness?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore, as a leading financial hub, is well-positioned to shape the carbon trading market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given our reputation for trust and competence, how is MTI nurturing a carbon trading ecosystem that leverages on Singapore’s strengths?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A key aspect of carbon trading is transferring international mitigation outcomes, requiring corresponding adjustments via G-to-G agreements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How is MTI collaborating with regional partners to develop beneficial frameworks?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While past Budgets have introduced grants for energy-efficient systems, will MTI enhance these grants to accelerate adoption?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the high energy consumption of large buildings, will MTI introduce grants for large building owners to drive meaningful energy savings?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specifically, as land intensification in business parks presents an opportunity to deploy district-wide energy solutions, such as district cooling, how is MTI ensuring that these projects incorporate energy efficiency targets at the design stage?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MTI has introduced several initiatives to enhance the business environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MTI provide an update on their impact on improving regulatory processes and benefiting businesses?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Collaboration between multinational enterprises (MNEs) and local businesses is key to scaling globally.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does the scheme require enhancements to strengthen the complementary relationship between MNEs and local enterprises and support local enterprises to scale globally?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the trend of onshoring and MNEs relocating key functions closer to home, how is MTI ensuring that MNE decision-makers remain in Singapore, enriching our business networks?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For local enterprises to scale, economies of scale are crucial.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I propose the existing merger and acquisitions (M&As) support programmes could be expanded to include joint ventures and shared services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, grant schemes, such as the Enterprise Development Grant and the Productivity Solutions Grant, could be restructured to offer higher grant quantums for joint enterprise development rather than individual efforts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tourism is a key pillar of Singapore’s economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can MTI provide an update on its progress and future efforts to keep Singapore competitive as a top global destination?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore’s local arts scene has immense potential to offer unique, authentic experiences for travellers seeking cultural depth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How is MTI working with local arts practitioners to integrate their content into tourism and enhance Singapore’s appeal to repeat visitors?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, the nightlife sector has faced significant challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nightlife is not only a lifestyle offering but also a complementary component of Singapore’s broader tourism experience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does STB view nightlife as an integral part of our tourism strategy?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If so, how is it supporting the industry to remain relevant and aligned with evolving consumer preferences?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By supporting startups, enhancing business networks, advancing sustainability and promoting tourism, we can cement Singapore's global hub status.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Singapore is home to some of the world's most innovative companies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To solidify our position as a global innovation hub, 2025 Budget introduced key initiatives to attract top entrepreneurial talent, deepen financial markets and drive research-led enterprise growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These measures will build upon Singapore's strengths as a global startup hub, where a business-friendly environment, world-class infrastructure and commitment to innovation have fostered a thriving deep-tech, fintech and research-driven ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, to sustain this momentum, we must ensure that startups at every stage of growth have the capital needed to scale successfully from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While we have a thriving early-stage funding ecosystem, high-growth companies often face challenges in securing capital to scale and expand.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I want to ask how will Singapore enhance venture capital participation, attract global investors and build a deeper late-stage financing ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, how will this programme be structured to qualify candidates?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: More importantly, how do we ensure these founders remain rooted in Singapore for the long term and contribute meaningfully to the broader enterprise ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will we embed them effectively into our economy?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must ensure these global founders choose to scale with Singapore rather than to relocate to larger markets once their ventures take flight.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, Singapore's commitment to research and development (R&D) has been a cornerstone of our economic strategy, keeping us competitive in an increasingly knowledge-driven global economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These sustained investments have positioned Singapore as a leader in key high-value sectors, including biotechnology and semi-conductors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Budget 2025 reinforces this commitment by further investing in R&D infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, while world-class infrastructure is essential, its full impact depends on a skilled workforce, the ability to commercialise research and strong industry adoption.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To fully realise the potential of these investments, we must address three critical factors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will the Government strengthen our talent pipeline to support these R&D facilities?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What measures will help translate research breakthroughs into viable industry applications?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will these facilities drive broader industry development and create opportunities for local enterprises to scale and compete globally?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: MNEs have long been a cornerstone of Singapore's economy, driving innovation, investment and job creation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They contribute significantly to GDP, high-value employment, R&D and global trade connectivity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, we must recognise the growing vulnerabilities associated with MNEs amid the shifting geopolitical dynamics.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These factors introduce uncertainties in the long-term business commitments and investment flows, posing challenges to Singapore's role as a strategic hub for global enterprises.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given these challenges, I ask the Minister: how will Singapore strengthen its value proposition to retain and attract MNEs?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What long-term strategies will ensure that we remain a critical global business hub despite shifting geopolitical currents?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Sir, strengthening Singapore's position as a global hub for startups and innovation will be key to driving competitiveness and increasing productivity.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With increasing global competition, we must continually enhance our startup ecosystem to remain at the forefront of innovation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: First, can MTI share how it intends to attract and support top-tier startups, specifically in deep-tech and sustainability sectors?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Second, how will MTI further strengthen funding access, talent attraction and market expansion support to help these companies grow and thrive in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, could we consider a regulatory sandbox model, allowing high-growth startups to test innovations under controlled conditions as we have already successfully done in the fintech industry?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This would empower Singapore-based companies to leverage homegrown innovation for growth by ensuring that local businesses are the primary beneficiaries of our research investments, we can strengthen our domestic innovation ecosystem and build globally competitive enterprises.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprise Singapore has a comprehensive set of schemes to help enterprises in their internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Amid the uncertain global economic environment including emerging protectionism, what are MTI's plans to ensure the schemes remain relevant in supporting local enterprises with the potential and desire to internationalise and grow?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: From the recent efforts in internationalisation, which sectors have fared well and continue to show scope for more companies to consider?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: From the recent efforts, have there been useful lessons that may benefit companies contemplating internationalisation given the increasingly crowded local domestic market in sectors, such as retail and food and beverage?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Will local lenders look favourably on funding internationalisation for local enterprises?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Enterprise Singapore has several schemes to help companies including SMEs in the internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MTI share how many companies have utilised these schemes and how successful their internationalisation efforts are?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Geopolitical uncertainties and trade tensions will have a significant impact on SMEs as they look to internationalise.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The threat of increased tariffs and regulatory compliance will mean higher cost and complexities for SMEs in their internationalisation efforts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Trade disputes will impact market access and cause supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will MTI ensure that the schemes remain relevant to support our local enterprises and what can be done to help SMEs mitigate the risks of internationalisation amidst the geopolitical uncertainties and trade tensions?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mark Lee, you can take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Singapore's economic success has always been built on our ability to connect with the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As a small market, our businesses must look outward to scale, compete and seize opportunities beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprise Singapore provides a comprehensive suite of schemes to support enterprises in their internationalisation efforts, but as global competition intensifies and economic uncertainties persist, we must ensure that our strategies remain agile and responsive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How is MTI ensuring that these schemes continue to be relevant and effective in helping local enterprise with the desire and potential to internationalise?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to enhance support for companies venturing into high-growth markets or navigating new trade barriers?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How will we position Singapore businesses to stay competitive globally while ensuring that they have the right resources and networks to succeed abroad?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For our local companies to scale and expand globally, access to capital is crucial.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could MTI share more details on how this fund will be structured and deployed to best support businesses?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Government consider the management of these funds with private sector players?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, what market gap does this fund seek to address and how will it complement existing financing schemes to enable more local enterprises to grow, internationalise and compete on a global stage?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: M&As should be seen as strategic growth engines for SMEs, enabling them to scale, innovate and compete effectively in regional and global markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, the high professional fees associated with M&A transactions covering advisory, due diligence and integration, often deter SMEs from pursuing such growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider introducing a new grant scheme or expanding the Enterprise Development Grant to help SMEs defray these costs, thereby encouraging more firms to explore M&A as a viable growth strategy?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond financial support, SMEs often struggle with articulating their valuations and long-term potential to potential partners and investors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To address this gap, could the Government collaborate with Trade Associations and Chambers to establish an Enterprise Financing Advisory Centre as a public-private partnership?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This centre could guide SMEs through the M&A process, equipping them with the expertise to structure deals effectively, secure suitable financing and maximise synergies post-merger.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, workforce transitions remain one of the most complex aspects of any merger, particularly for SMEs with limited HR and change management resources.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This would help SMEs retain valuable talent while ensuring that workforce restructuring does not become a barrier to M&A-driven growth.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By strengthening financial, advisory and workforce support mechanisms, we can foster an environment where M&A is not just an option for SMEs, but a strategic enabler of growth and transformation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has introduced various funding measures to support businesses in adopting AI and digitalisation, helping them transform their processes and systems.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, beyond financial support, SMEs often require deeper guidance to fully integrate these technologies into their operations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How are MTI and other agencies ensuring that SMEs can effectively utilise the Enterprise Compute Initiative scheme, particularly in leveraging AI and digital tools to enhance productivity and competitiveness?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, businesses, especially SMEs can benefit from AI adoption to enhance efficiency by streamlining business processes and reducing the need for manual interventions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: AI tools can enable the analysis of vast amounts of data to provide insights to allow businesses to uncover trends and valuable insights to better understand customers, predict market trends, optimise supply chains.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This allows for more informed decision-making and operational efficiency.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: AI can help catalyse innovation and provide competitive advantage by creating new products, services and processes that drive growth and competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But AI adoption can be challenging for SMEs as it can be expensive, and SMEs have limited budgets and lack specialised skills and may not have quality data and large datasets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: For businesses to truly reap the benefits of AI solutions, fostering a culture of innovation is essential.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It is imperative to rethink and redesign processes and implement new workflows.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There are many schemes to support businesses to adopt AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What impact has AI helped to achieve for businesses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, by leveraging AI and Government business data, we can proactively prequalify SMEs and invite them to apply for the relevant assistance schemes, thus removing the guesswork and streamlining support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Chairman, with more than 80% of Singaporeans residing in the heartlands, our heartlands are not just merely residential zones, but the essence of our nation’s identity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Last year, we saw the introduction of the Heartland Enterprise Placemaking Grant (HEPG).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: For example, Quan Shui Wet Market received the HEPG.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is a third-generation wet market business that has expanded into a fresh food grocer and now serves over 500 households daily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The company, which currently does not have presence in the east of Singapore, tapped on the scheme to gain exposure and market insights on residents in the east at the Marine Parade’s Easty Breezy Bazaar.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Considering the sheer number of heartland merchants in Singapore, it might seem that 40 expressions of interest for the scheme might need further enhancements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Could the Ministry share how many heartland merchants have successfully secured the HEPG as of date, and what outcomes might be observed in terms of business growth and community engagement for these merchants?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Has there also been feedback from stakeholders on how the scheme can be enhanced?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Could the Ministry also provide an update on the effectiveness and outreach of its initiatives promoting the vibrancy of heartland businesses?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: As we commemorate SG60 this year, let us restate our commitment to ensuring our heartlands remain dynamic, vibrant and reflective of the Singaporean spirit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Hence, we must provide our local businesses with the help they need to enable them to help themselves ensure the viability and sustainability of their trades.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Mr Chairman, MTI and EnterpriseSG launched the Heartland Enterprise Placemaking Grant in 2024.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Could MTI provide an update on the response to this grant from the merchants and how many applications have been received and how many have been approved.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Based on activities and events organised thus far, how has the response been from residents and the wider community?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Have merchants benefited from increased footfall and business growth?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Key to all business is staying relevant and competitive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: The alternatives, such as large malls located in the heartlands, also draw significant footfall.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua
text: Will there be regular reviews to ensure this scheme achieves the intended outcomes?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Chairman, Sir, the Tourism 2040 roadmap is aimed at setting out Singapore’s long-term strategy to drive quality tourism growth and strengthen our position as a leading global destination.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: As mentioned by Minister Chee, Changi Airport's upcoming T5 will enhance our capacity to handle up to 50 million additional passengers annually.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Given these developments, could MTI provide an update on the progress of our tourism development efforts?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Also, what strategies are in place to refresh our tourism and lifestyle experiences, ensuring Singapore remains an attractive destination amidst growing global competition?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One immediate area of interest to local artists is that of affordable studio spaces.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard of Singapore artists seeking rental spaces in Johor Baru due to high costs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, one common refrain in the local art scene is that the artwork produced locally tends to be small in size, simply because artists cannot afford large studio spaces for production.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could there also be bilateral initiatives, such as cross-border artist residencies, public art projects, or co-organised arts festivals, to connect Singapore and Malaysian creatives into the larger regional arts ecosystem?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives could well be integrated into the economic sector of tourism which has been identified as an area for potential cooperation between the two countries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As we develop the JS-SEZ together with our partners, it is important that arts and culture are not sidelined in favour of purely commercial interests.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that MTI can work with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, and the arts community to explore ways to leverage this partnership so that we can support artists in securing affordable workspaces and good cross-border creative opportunities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Ministry can consider these suggestions and provide updates on its plans for Singapore's creative industries in the development of the JS-SEZ.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My second cut is on Singapore’s future plans for music festivals.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These festivals serve as an important meeting point for musicians, industry professionals, fans and the general public to create meaningful shared experiences and a lasting sense of community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They also offer substantial economic and soft power benefits.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that our regional neighbours have managed to successfully harness.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Thailand’s Wonderfruit Festival, for instance, has evolved into a globally acclaimed event, attracting international visitors and elevating the country’s cultural prominence.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a widely held impression in the public sphere that the music festival scene in Singapore is far less vibrant than it was some years ago.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To be clear, in my use of the term “music festival” I am referring to outdoor music events with a running theme, featuring more than three acts, and fringe activities like food and beverage stalls or artwork displays.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It features mostly niche local and regional acts, as well as free admission.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that there has been some recent movement in the scene.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is promising and I have four questions on the Ministry’s future plans.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, has any funding been allocated for the development of these music festivals under the tourism development funds or otherwise?

speaker: The Chairman
text: You can take your two cuts as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Chairman, Singapore has set an ambitious goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, but we must ensure that our transition to a low-carbon economy does not come at the expense of our competitiveness, especially as Singapore faces intensifying regional competition.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Many of our regional peers are also advancing their sustainability agendas, but they are doing so while keeping energy costs low and maintaining a strong industrial base.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Can MTI provide an update on its measures to transition to a low-carbon economy, particularly in decarbonising the power sector while ensuring that energy remains cost-competitive for businesses?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: How will Singapore strike the right balance between sustainability and economic viability, ensuring that our industries remain attractive for investment and job creation, even as we push for green transformation?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: For Singapore to move forward, businesses must integrate sustainability into their operations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: The Sustainability Reporting Grant and Singapore Emission Factor Registry, launched by SBF, have been instrumental in simplifying sustainability reporting.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: However, businesses, especially SMEs, continue to face challenges due to the complexity and resource-intensive nature of reporting requirements.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Additionally, SMEs often lack inhouse expertise to navigate sustainability requirements.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Could the Government work with trade associations and chambers to develop a step-by-step decarbonisation roadmap, equipping SMEs with clear guidance on sustainability adoption?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Next Member is not here, Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The transition to a low-carbon economy, bolstered energy security and an increased supply of green energy are pivotal to sustaining and advancing our digital economy and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As digital technologies, particularly AI, become more integrated horizontally and vertically across industries and sectors, the demand for data centres and higher computing power will increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: The consequent demand for energy will also rise exponentially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Such a surge is attributed to the accelerating deployment of AI technologies and proliferation of digital services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Further, training advanced AI models requires substantial computational power, also leading to heightened energy demands.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For example, processing a unit of text in Gen AI models can emit a carbon footprint comparable to driving a gasoline-powered vehicle for five to 20 miles.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Hence, integrating green and clean energy sources into the digital economy is crucial.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We will also have to diversity our energy sources to guard against geopolitical uncertainties and ensure our energy security.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Thus, can MTI update on its measures to transition Singapore to a low-carbon economy, including the decarbonisation of the power sector?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How does the Government also intend to leverage our position as a financial hub and robust financial infrastructure to support our transition to a low carbon economy and securing green energy for our future needs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How does the Government plan to more actively participate in the carbon markets and position ourselves as a credible, vibrant, highly liquid and highly connected hub for carbon credit markets?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: And in doing so, how does the Government see itself partnering private companies, big and small, in achieving these aims?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As a small resource constraint country, Singapore imports almost all of our energy needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Ensuring stable and secure energy sources while transitioning to clean energy is a challenge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can MTI provide an update on the measures to transition to a low carbon economy, including decarbonising the power sector?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What trade-offs will Singapore need to consider as we transition?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can MTI share more details on Singapore's nuclear strategy and plans including safety, reliability and environmental impact of the deployment of nuclear.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is more than just a technological investment – it strengthens energy security, economic resilience and environmental responsibility.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As Singapore explores sustainable energy solutions, small modular reactors have emerged as a potential long-term option for clean and reliable power.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given rapid advancements in small modular reactor technology globally, how will the fund be deployed to assess its feasibility for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What steps are being taken to enhance research, regulatory readiness and talent development?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we working with international partners to accelerate learning and preparedness?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we move swiftly from exploration to pilot programs and, ultimately, full-scale deployment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can MTI update on its measures to transition to a low carbon economy, including by decarbonising the power sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Following the award of Conditional Approvals for multiple projects to import low carbon electricity from Indonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia, and even Australia , can MTI share what infrastructure is required to ensure imported energy sources are seamlessly fed into the Singapore energy grid in future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We are also exploring the feasibility of alternatives such as nuclear power or hydrogen power plants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Considering the topped-up Future Energy Fund, what is the impact of decarbonisation on Singaporeans from an energy pricing perspective?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and hydrogen play a big part in our energy future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While we continue on our energy transition to low carbon energy, we must also ensure our energy security in the midst of increasing geopolitical tension and increasing electricity consumption year-on-year – with the exception of 2020 when COVID-19 hit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How relevant is LNG for Singapore, in terms of energy security?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry Gan Kim Yong.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Chairman, let me first thank Members for their very constructive comments and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The year 2024 has been a relatively good year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have come a long way in building a strong, innovative and vibrant economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have created good opportunities for Singaporeans and improved their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our economic success did not happen by chance.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It was the result of a combination of factors: careful long-term planning; sustained investments in infrastructure; keeping a pro-business environment; and, most important of all, investing in lifelong education and training, together with staying open to talent, trade and investment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Generations of Singaporeans have worked together to build a strong foundation for our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But Members are well aware that we are now entering a new chapter in our economic journey with new challenges and opportunities unlike those we have seen before.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the potential headwinds arising from geopolitical contestation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members would have heard United States (US) President Donald Trump's new tariffs and his plans for more, including reciprocal tariffs on trading partners to match the duties on US' exports.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: China and Canada have also responded with their own tariffs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This may lead to an escalating, tit-for-tat cycle for tariffs, or worse, a global trade war.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This could upend the global rules-based economic order that Singapore, as a small and open economy, is dependent on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Given that we do not impose tariffs on any American imports and the US has a trade surplus with us, we may not be significantly affected by the reciprocal tariffs directly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, rising tariffs and trade wars could cause disruptions to supply chains, slow down global trade and drive up business costs, and therefore, affect businesses and consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the longer term, it will also affect confidence and investment flows and slow down the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Instead of seeking win-win opportunities with their partners, many countries are now competing aggressively against each other for investments and protecting their domestic sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will lead to a more challenging external environment for us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Domestically, we will also need to tackle tighter constraints, especially in land, labour and carbon I spoke about last year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our local workforce growth is expected to continue to slow in the coming years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With limited land, we will need to find new ways to maximise our space utilisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To do our part on climate change, we will need to reduce our carbon footprint while accommodating the growing energy demand as we expand our industries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nevertheless, it is not all doom and gloom.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Amidst these challenges, there are still opportunities for us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Asia's economy will continue to grow and Southeast Asia is expected to become the fourth largest economy in the world by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI), digitalisation and the low-carbon transition will also present new opportunities in the digital and green economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if we can grow faster.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will certainly try to do so and we hope we can grow faster than what we have projected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Last year, I spoke about four strategies to allow us to grow, namely, grow our economy; unlock our resource potential; transform our businesses; and connect internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will speak about how we will grow our economy while my colleagues will elaborate on the other strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how Singapore can strengthen regional trade relations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will benefit our firms here by allowing them to tap on the resources available in Johor to expand and grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: JS-SEZ will also allow Singapore and Malaysia to draw in investments, by offering a more compelling value proposition by combining our complementary strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have seen strong commercial interest in JS-SEZ.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Singapore Business Federation's business mission to Johor Bahru last month drew 230 delegates from over 180 Singapore businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also continue to build on our existing cooperation with Indonesia, particularly in Batam, Bintan and Karimun, as well as explore new areas of cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will accelerate the growth of the digital economy within ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also plan to conclude negotiations and sign the upgrade to the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) this year, which will boost intra-ASEAN trade and strengthen supply chain connectivity within our region, to tap on the growth of Asia's economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we deepen our connections, we want to nurture Singapore enterprises to become regional or global leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also seek to anchor global industry leaders here to enhance our industry ecosystems, which will benefit local companies and provide good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Neil Parekh have noted, innovation is at the heart of economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, over the past decades, we have successfully built up a strong and competitive semi-conductor ecosystem that has cemented Singapore as a critical node in the global semi-conductor supply chain.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But to remain a semi-conductor powerhouse, we must invest in research and development (R&D) to drive innovation within the industry, not just among the big players but also among the small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Semi-conductor manufacturing facilities typically involve substantial upfront investments.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Companies, especially the smaller ones, may face challenges accessing semi-conductor infrastructure and expertise in their R&D and pilot production.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To support them, we established the National Semiconductor Translation and Innovation Centre (NSTIC) last April, at the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: NSTIC provides companies and researchers in the fields of flat optics and silicon photonics with access to semi-conductor R&D infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Companies may also tap NSTIC's capabilities for prototyping and small volume manufacturing to accelerate the speed to market and scaling up.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will offer state-of-the-art cleanroom infrastructure and industry-grade tools, as well as translational research and fabrication expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will support the scaling and translation of R&D.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Major global semi-conductor players as well as SMEs and startups can tap on its capabilities and even foster new partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One example is NexGen Wafer Systems, a local SME which supplies wet etching and cleaning equipment to chipmakers worldwide.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They had started their R&D efforts overseas to better access tools and facilities that were not available in Singapore then.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: By leveraging A*STAR's R&D capabilities and facilities, NexGen has developed new semi-conductor equipment features and applications in Singapore to fabricate different types of chips.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They have therefore found value in bringing a part of their R&D activities back to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our R&D efforts have also enabled us to develop a strong pipeline of promising and innovative startups.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One example is Lucence, an A*STAR spin-off and homegrown startup.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Lucence focuses on precision oncology and partners the National Cancer Centre to develop the LiquidHALLMARK test to guide therapy selection for tumours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With support from Enterprise Singapore, Lucence automated its Singapore laboratory to serve customers in Singapore, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It partnered Mayo Clinic Laboratories this year, to drive adoption and commercialisation of its technology in US.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Today, Singapore also hosts many Deep Tech companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Among them is Entropica Labs, a startup from the Centre for Quantum Technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Entropica Labs has been working with global leaders in quantum computing hardware and infrastructure providers, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Xanadu, to bring quantum technologies to the market.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to do more through the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA) nodes in key innovation hubs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We help our companies tap into the innovation networks and market opportunities overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Carecam, a digital health startup focusing on transitional care and advanced screening, participated in the GIA San Francisco Acceleration Programme and connected with a US-based corporate to integrate their solutions into new business entities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will support the company's expansion into the US healthcare sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The GIA Discovery will support startups to familiarise themselves with the market and evaluate product-market fit, in order to shape their market strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Thereafter, startups can pilot their technologies in these new markets, with the support from GIA Proof of Concept to validate their products and gain market credibility.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The GIA+ initiative will support startups participating in global acceleration programmes, such as those run by Y Combinator, MassRobotics and MassChallenge in the US, to gain access to mentorship, resources and networks to realise their overseas expansion plans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To expand our startup ecosystem, we also want experienced founders to be anchored here and build their new ventures that have the potential to become globally leading businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is a targeted programme aimed at supporting the new ventures of experienced founders from around the world as well as in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Founders are individuals who have built highly successful startups or who have developed major new products and business lines in global companies, or who have made significant scientific or engineering achievements, such as in AI or Deep Tech.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The GFP signals our belief in the power of openness.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to bring the best from around the world to Singapore to add to the strength of our own.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to support firms which are able and willing to innovate and grow.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will foster a vibrant innovation ecosystem that will help our companies stay competitive and create high-value job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It also supports the growth of the financial and professional services sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Last October, I attended KLA's groundbreaking ceremony for a new manufacturing facility in Singapore, for some of their most advanced wafer geometry and defect inspection tools.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will also create opportunities for enterprises here to collaborate with KLA on niche areas, such as precision cleaning and manufacturing of metal parts used in optics assemblies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, local SME Alantac Industrial Services and KLA co-developed precision cleaning solutions for defect inspection tools that meet stringent cleaning requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
