text: On the multilateral front, Singapore co-convenes the World Trade Organization (WTO) Joint Statement Initiative on E-Commerce with Australia and Japan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This helps establish global rules in digital trade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And after five years of negotiations, we reached an agreement on the text last year, supported by around 70 members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are working to incorporate the agreement into the WTO and expand its membership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are also advancing our Green Economy Agreements (GEAs) to catalyse collaborations in green innovation and trade flows in sustainable products, and ultimately accelerate our low-carbon transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Under our GEA with Australia, we established a co-innovation programme for SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We call this the Go Green Co-Innovation Programme (GGCIP) to incentivise partnerships between Australian and Singapore enterprises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The programme has supported five projects, including the joint venture between Singapore-based ESGpedia and Australia's FootprintLab, to develop an AI-powered sustainability reporting tool to help businesses with climate disclosure and sustainable supply chain management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In November, we also launched a joint working group on trade and the green economy with New Zealand and Chile, with plans to enhance cross-border trade and investment in green growth areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Chairman, our iconic Singapore River is a symbol of our nation's success story – a dynamic hub that facilitates the seamless flow of people, trade and capital through our shores and as a gateway for the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Together, we will grow our economy, unlock new potential, transform enterprises and connect Singapore to the world, ensuring our collective success as we chart a bold course forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Gan, in his speech and in response to my query, mentioned that the worst case scenario for Singapore amidst an ongoing US-China contestation could be a global trade war.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to further ask the Deputy Prime Minister what Singapore is doing to mitigate that potential impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And also, if I can ask the Deputy Prime Minister to share how he sees our relationship with US and with China, whether in the event of a global trade war, would that put us in a better position to manage the downsides?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This way, we can then continue to expand and grow our economic space in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I mentioned, it is a fast-growing area and I think we will continue to work with the ASEAN partners to see how we can deepen our integration within ASEAN so that we have more opportunities for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at the same time, as I mentioned in my speech, we continue to expand our collaboration with our neighbours particularly, and see how we can leverage on each other's strengths so that when we combine together, we have a a better value proposition for our trading partners and our business partners globally.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But also it is important for us to explore new areas of growth and opportunities for collaboration.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, I mentioned about digital economy, which is a new platform.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is not the same as traditional FTAs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is not just about tariffs and imports or exports, but it is about collaboration and interoperability in developing the digital capability to strengthen our own enterprises, giving them the better opportunity to expand in the region.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think this is something that we will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And we have to continue to remain nimble and to monitor the development.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And I am sure every Member, and nowadays, when you wake up in the morning, open the newspaper, the first thing you see is what are the major news.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And every time, you are shocked into waking up with the news.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And now, without reading the newspaper, you can read it on your mobile phone, and these are news alerts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And I think you just have to take it when it comes and always be nimble, be prepared to move very quickly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This also speaks to the strength of Singapore as a small economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are able to a very compact economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are able to move very quickly, we are able to respond very fast.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is important for us to work closely with the enterprises and with our businesses through the various trade associations and organisations to see how we can bring our businesses along.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Keep them informed on the developments around the world, enable them and equip them so that they are able to adjust their supply chains, their production lines and their export markets quite quickly.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, it is important for us to continue to invest in our people so that they acquire new skills and new capabilities because as the global economy changes, new opportunities will emerge.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we must have the skills to be able to tap into these opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, I think getting our industries and enterprises to be nimble and move fast, investing in training of our people, these are fundamentals to keep Singapore's economy resilient and continue to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My clarification relates to supporting SMEs in terms of internationalising, and it is for Minister of State Tan.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He shared on SGProtein and how it has enhanced its competitiveness in the Korean market by tapping the FTAs, and he has also shared on the many FTAs that we are working on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can more be shared on how the Government and SBF are working together to support our SMEs in terms of better tapping these FTAs and getting access to new markets?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, it is not just enough for us to expand our FTAs and sign these FTAs even in far flung countries, it is also important for us to work very closely with our business associations, like SBF and others, to take them there and show them what the business opportunities are.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And also, while they are in Singapore, to give them the tools and the support for them to take up these advantages as they look at how to lower their costs and increase their business efficiency.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are a few things maybe I want to just share with Ms Jessica Tan.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, it helps them to navigate this and then test how much they would have to pay, for example, or how they can increase their efficiency.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: SBF has been working very closely with us to provide companies like SGProtein with on-site guidance on, for example, how even to produce and prepare a manufacturing cost statement application.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: CFOTI helps businesses address issues related to trade compliance and also expands the capacity to benefit on trade agreements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are also bespoke advisory support through this, for our SMEs to make the best use of FTAs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I encourage our SMEs to work closely with us, Enterprise Singapore, as well as our trade associations, like SBF, to fully utilise these FTAs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I think from the announcements today, it truly shows that when there are constructive comments, the Government is not tone deaf but is actually tuned in to make sure that Singapore remains agile and business-friendly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For this AFA, I would like to ask for the Government to consider continuing this platform from time to time, so as to reinforce the strong partnership between the Government and the business community.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is definitely a good opportunity and an important source of alternative financing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: There are currently already many private credit fund providers, mainly catering to larger MNEs and large local corporates, and often leave their local enterprises underserved.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We also want to thank the 13 TACs that joined us in this journey from February to November last year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We consulted many of the businesses, not just sectoral but also the industry and trade associations and so on.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That really is the usual engagement, and we must continue to sustain this momentum.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That is why earlier, during Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong's speech, you heard him mentioning that he helms the Inter-Ministerial Committee for Pro-Enterprise Rules Review.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to reassure Mr Mark Lee and in fact, the business community that MTI and not just MTI, now that we have set up the SME PEO from 26 March onwards as a key coordination unit to galvanise the whole-of-Government to lean forward, to continue to work with the business sector to improve the regulatory agility, to better support our businesses to seize opportunities overseas.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There is a second part of the question that maybe I can address – the suggestion about the Private Credit Growth Fund.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is a scheme that is designed to fill the gap in the financing framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have equity financing, we have the normal commercial loans, but some of these high-growth companies are in a very niche area and they are not able to find financing so easily available.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And the owners, the entrepreneurs, are also not keen to be diluted.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: They want to retain control of their businesses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, equity investment may not be suitable for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This private credit allows more flexibility for the structure of the financing to be designed to suit the needs of the specific companies.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is not meant to be a subsidy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It is not meant to be for businesses that are having difficulties or need subsidies or support for overseas expansion.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I have mentioned some of them, like GIA and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These are other schemes that will support businesses going overseas, expanding their regional presence, even including R&D funds and efforts and so on.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, there are different schemes designed for different purposes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For this particular private credit scheme, it is really meant to fill a gap in the financing framework.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I just want to thank the whole MTI team for a very comprehensive analysis and presentation and a very detailed Budget – a very good Budget in my view.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister spoke about the NSTIC (R&D Fab) to drive advanced semi-conductor research and innovation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: What is the immediate benefit to our local semi-conductor system with this NSTIC (R&D Fab)?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The second question is: we have seen newspaper reports recently on NTUC researchers discovering a geothermal reservoir in Yishun.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps MTI can provide an update on its study on the potential of geothermal energy going forward.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on private credit, having spent part of my life in the business, I think $1 billion will be too small.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the purpose should be to use that as a base to harness external funds and perhaps make that $10 billion or more going forward.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: So, serving that as $1 billion from MTI, with $9 billion raised from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The idea is to increase the density and advanced packaging plays a very important role in allowing that to happen.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is a key fundamental foundational technology.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We started investing in this technology since 2011 and we have built a significant capability in this area.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will keep our options open and keep our doors open, and we welcome other emerging technologies which may become important and critical for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will also make these facilities available to other companies which have emerging technologies to invest in R&D.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I presume he is talking about the Private Credit Growth Fund.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will be very happy if we can talk to Mr Neil Parekh to raise the other $9 billion, if he can help us do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I must say that, generally, I think this is the seed money the Government has to put in.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will keep our doors open for private credit which wants to come in and to join us in this journey.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As I mentioned in my speech, when fund managers and investors are more familiar in this space of private credit, we may then be able to catalyse more funds from outside.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We look at this $1 billion as seed money.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We hope to be able to raise even more capital in time to come for this fund.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But I think this is a good start.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the Member was referring to Nanyang Technological University's (NTU's) study, not "NTUC".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think we will be dealing a lot with NTUC later on in MOM's COS debate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In NTUC, it is – just for the benefit of all my brothers and sisters in NTUC – every worker matters, not every power source matters.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think we all know Singapore, as a country, we are alternative energy-disadvantaged and I have mentioned many times in the past that we will explore every possible decarbonisation pathway.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the indigenous energy options that we have, that we are investigating is geothermal energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In 2023, EMA issued a request for proposal for a Singapore-wide non-invasive geophysical study to assess Singapore's deep geothermal resource potential at depths of up to 10 kilometres.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is for the purpose of power generation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I want to emphasise, EMA is to assess the deep geothermal resource potential.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We hope and we aim to complete this study in about a year's time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Again, like I said, in terms of giving a very clear demarcation, NTU's study focuses on establishing the localised potential at areas surveyed up to a depth of about four kilometres.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whereas ours is the deep sort of geothermal assessment, which is up to 10 kilometres.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, given the fact that we have an existing Sembawang hot spring, I know that many of my comrades are also concerned about how that would impact Sembawang.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Singapore Government, let me reassure everyone, is not conducting any invasive geophysical studies that could affect the existing hot spring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The geothermal drillings have been carried out by NTU sites.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They were at sites that were 2.5 kilometres and 700 metres away, almost a kilometre away from the Sembawang hot spring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our EMA's ongoing studies, they are non-invasive because we are conducting airborne and land-based surveys of our entire country's geophysical landscape for a better assessment of the deep geothermal potential.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As with every study, every new infrastructural development that we undertake, all of the necessary environmental assessments will be conducted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope I have given Members enough reassurance as well as understanding of what we know thus far.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I have two clarifications for Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling on my cut on scams, which she touched on briefly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, she mentioned the whole-of-Government efforts through the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Scams (IMCS).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it doing anything in the field of online scams to protect consumers or to do some standard setting?

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Chairman, I want to thank Ms Sylvia Lim for her two clarifications.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I understand where the Member is coming from when she shared her thinking when she delivered her cut yesterday.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As shared by Minister of State Sun Xueling during the Ministry of Home Affair's (MHA's) COS debate, a majority of the scams involve self-effected transfers of money to scammers as well as cryptocurrency scams.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: These are, one, criminal in nature and two, often carried out by highly sophisticated criminal networks.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The third point really is that a lot of these are really based out of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, such scams are, hence, more appropriately handled by our law enforcement authorities.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But I want to assure her that to ensure a collective effort in tackling scams, the Singapore Government works closely not just mounting a whole-of-Government approach, but also with the private sector.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI sits in, and if there are relevant cases that are relevant to our economic agency, that is where we will bridge the communications.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This really forms part of the whole-of-Government approach, where agencies can work together to safeguard consumer interest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, I have two questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister spoke about R&D infrastructure in Singapore and how it is important as part of our economic growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I spoke about this during my COS cut where I said that equally important is R&D being commercialised.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister how specifically local enterprises will benefit with all the R&D spent, how are we going to encourage them to take this up, how are we going to encourage and support them to really take this R&D and commercialise it into applications?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second one I just like to weigh in to hon Member Neil Parekh's comment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I probably take the other end of conservatism.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: He talked to balance the ambition; I think private credit is quite a science, related to a lot of risk management as well, if Government is going to go into this.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Traditionally, when we co-fund, the bank comes in and you risk-share.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I would very much like to know that given that it is not small sum, $1 billion that the Government is going into, how is this going to be underwritten, in terms of risk management?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How are you going to pick which company you are going to back pick?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Because $1 billion will not go very far and we want to make sure that this is a good experience and that we can bag more companies?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, which agency is going to administer this and the partnerships?

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because the facilities are very costly and very expensive; the SMEs will not be able to have access to these facilities, other than through NSTIC.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, that is one area that we do.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A*STAR does the same for many other domains in the industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, we partner our private sector to allow them to have access R&D facilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But it is not just the hardware facilities, because NSTIC and A*STAR also provide consultancy advice on how to do their R&D from a technical point but, at the same time, how to commercialise their products.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also have a collaboration with IHLs through our technology transfer officers to help companies on to how to translate their technology into commercial products.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There are many platforms to allow us to work in partnership with our companies to commercialise their R&D efforts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: One other aspect of the at NSTIC, which I mentioned in my speech, is the collaboration between the MNCs and the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because they are able to work together, the SMEs will understand the needs of the larger companies to develop their products to be able to serve the MNCs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This also encourages a collaboration between MNCs, which have more resources, and to help the SMEs to also commercialise their R&D products.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We hope the Member can collectively persuade Ministry of Finance to give us a bit more in time to come.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are approaching the end of our guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Because you had four cuts, so I will give you the floor.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I have just one quick clarification for Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had filed a cut on the infrastructure for energy source, in terms of energy infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister shared earlier about the hydrogen strategy and the ammonia strategy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can Minister share about what our budgeting plans for power sourcing infrastructure in terms of landing points?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I know ammonia and hydrogen and nuclear is still at the research phase and we are still investigating on those.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But how are our plans of planning or investing on infrastructure for those, including the landing points for imported energy sources?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And the interconnectors, for the landing sites, we have preliminarily identified some of the sites, the details of which I am not at liberty to reveal at this point in time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the interconnectors, broadly, there are two types – the high voltage direct current, which entails significantly longer distance traversing the subsea distances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And then, you have the relatively less expensive alternating current type of subsea cable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, depending on the site, the source of the generation of that renewable energy source, the appropriate type of cable would be utilised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those would involve higher cost cable, involving high voltage direct current subsea cables.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That covers one big part of renewable energy imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the carbon capture storage, we are still studying the model working with the S-Hub.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Looking at the aggregation of the hard to abate carbon intensive sectors, this would be quite a fair bit of the petrochemical industry on Jurong Island.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Looking at the transportation and, eventually, the storage of the carbon that we have captured, at this point in time, given the amounts that are involved, we are still working with some of the potential partners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For ammonia and hydrogen, I have also stated earlier on that hydrogen, at this point in time, even though it is a technically feasible pathway, the transportation of hydrogen, by itself, is very costly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are using ammonia as a pilot.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have a pathfinder project where we are going to work with a couple of potential consortia to work out when it comes of scale, whether it would be a feasible and a commercially viable pathway.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are looking, as a pilot pathfinder, about between 50 to 60 megawatts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will provide initial seed funding to assess the viability of that pathway.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The sum of it all is that we have set aside the budget.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, given the different thresholds that we have not arrived at yet, the drawdown from the FEF is still not there.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we have topped it up because we envisage that in the coming quarters ahead, once we cross certain key thresholds, the drawdown will happen.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can I invite Mr Liang, if you would like to draw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Chairman, allow me to thank Deputy Prime Minister Gan, Minister Tan See Ling, Senior Minister of State Low Yen Ling and Minister of State Alvin Tan for their very thorough responses to our cuts and clarifications.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: It leaves me to just wish the MTI family every success in growing our economy, hopefully, once again, to outperform our forecasted range of 1% to 3% growth for 2025.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 2.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.27 pm until 2.45 pm.
